vignette:
David always took pride in his hands. They were large, calloused, and strong-the hands of a man who had built a life from nothing. He'd left Ghana at twenty-two with a nascent skill in pipe-fitting and an abundance of determination. For nearly thirty years in America, those hands had fixed leaks, installed water heaters, and unclogged the drains of a thousand homes. They had provided for his wife, Ama, and their two children, now grown. His work as a plumber was more than a job; it was a testament to his capability, his reliability. He was the man you called when something was broken, and he always knew how to make it right.

That sense of order and competence was shattered on a Tuesday afternoon eight months ago. It was a routine call, a clogged drain in the basement of a well-kept house in a quiet, leafy suburb. He'd finished the job and was packing his tools when he heard footsteps on the stairs. He turned, expecting the homeowner, but was met by two young men he'd never seen before. There was no demand, no warning-just a sudden, violent shove from behind.

He remembers the cold shock of the concrete floor against his cheek and the coppery taste of blood in his mouth. The attack was a blur of kicks, of sharp, radiating pain in his ribs and head. More than the physical pain, he remembers the feeling of utter helplessness, the grating sound of their laughter as they took his wallet and the watch Ama had given him for their anniversary. They were gone in less than a minute, leaving him on the floor of a stranger's basement, surrounded by the tools he could no longer grip.

In the beginning, everyone was kind. Ama was a fortress of support, the police were respectful, and his clients sent get-well cards. The physical wounds healed; the bruises faded and the fractured rib mended. But something inside David remained broken. Sleep became a battlefield. He'd jolt awake in a cold sweat, the phantom sensation of a boot connecting with his side echoing through his body. He started sleeping on the sofa, telling Ama his snoring was too loud, but the truth was he couldn't bear to be touched unexpectedly in the dark.

His work, once a source of pride, became a minefield of triggers. Every time he had to take a job in a basement, a cold dread would seep into his bones. The dim lighting, the smell of damp earth and concrete-it all transported him back to that floor. He'd find himself constantly looking over his shoulder, his heart hammering in his chest at the sound of footsteps overhead. He began turning down jobs that required him to work in enclosed, isolated spaces, making excuses about his schedule or a bad back. The calls started to dwindle.

At home, the man Ama married was disappearing. He was quiet, his easy laughter replaced by a constant, simmering irritability. A misplaced set of keys or a burnt piece of toast could unleash a torrent of anger that left the whole house walking on eggshells. He stopped cooking his favorite Ghanaian dishes, the smells and spices no longer bringing him joy. He felt a profound sense of detachment from his own family, watching them from behind a thick wall of glass. He saw their concern, their love, but he couldn't feel it. He just felt shame. A man, a husband, a father, was supposed to be strong. He was supposed to protect. A man was not supposed to be so easily broken by two boys in a stranger's basement.

Now, he spends most days in his truck, parked at a nearby park, watching other people live their lives. He tells Ama he's going to a job, but he can't bring himself to answer the phone when it rings. His hands, the instruments of his livelihood and identity, often rest trembling in his lap. He looks at them and no longer sees a master plumber, a provider, or a builder. He sees only the man who was left helpless on a cold, concrete floor.
